## Data Structures

-   vectors

-   factors

-   lists

-   matrices

-   arrays

-   ***`dataframes`***

## Dataframe

The dataframe is the most "complex", useful and powerful structure in R. Intuitively it is an excel sheet, while from R's point of view it is a type of **list** with some properties/restrictions

-   each element of the list is a **vector** with an **associated name** (aka a column)
-   each list/column must have the same number of elements
-   as a consequence, each row has the same number of elements (**rectangular structure**)

## Creation

Most of the time you will import dataframes rather than create them, but it is important to first understand how they work and how to create/manipulate them. They are created with the `data.frame` command

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Create a dataframe with 3 columns
my_df <- data.frame( col1 = 1:4, col2 = letters[1:4],
                    col3 = rnorm(n = 4, mean = 0, sd = 1))
my_df
```

## Attributes

The **`dataframe`** has both the attributes of a list, i.e. the ***names***, and the attributes of a matrix, i.e. the ***dimensions*** (rows and columns)

```{r, echo=TRUE}
attributes(my_df)
dim(my_df)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

As with the other structures we have seen, we can use the functions **`names()`** , **`dim()`**, **`nrow()`**, **`ncol()`**... to get information about the properties of the dataframe. 

```{r,echo=TRUE}
names(iris) # iris is a dataset available by default in R (?iris)
nrow(iris)
ncol(iris)
```

----

The most useful function is **`str()`**, since it gives us a quick overview of the structure of the dataframe: dimensions, variable types,...

```{r,echo=TRUE}
str(iris) 
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Indexing

We can use either square brackets **`[]`**:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
my_df
my_df[1]  # extract a 4x1 data.frame
```

---

```{r, echo = TRUE}
my_df[[1]] # extract the first column of the data.frame
my_df[1,1] # extract the first element of the first column of the data.frame
```

---

...or the dollar sign **`$`**

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# my_df[[1]] equivalent
my_df$col1 # extract the first column of the data.frame
```

... extract the first element of the first column...
```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_df$col1[1] 
```

## Indexing - Relational operators

One of the most common operations you will deal with is extracting/evaluating a subset of the values in your dataset:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_df

# keep only the rows where the values of column1 are greater than 2
my_df[my_df$col1 > 2, ] # = my_df[my_df[1] > 2, ]

```

## Examples

```{r}
my_df
```

::: fragment
```{r, echo=TRUE,eval=FALSE}
my_df[my_df$col1 > 2 & my_df$col1 < 4, ]
```
:::

::: fragment
```{r, eval=TRUE}
my_df[my_df$col1 > 2 & my_df$col1 < 4, ]
```
:::

::: fragment
```{r, echo=TRUE,eval=FALSE}
my_df[my_df$col1== 2,  2]
```
:::

::: fragment
```{r, eval=TRUE}
my_df[my_df$col1== 2,  2]
```
:::

::: fragment
```{r, echo=TRUE,eval=FALSE}
my_df[my_df$col1== 2,  "col2"]
```
:::

::: fragment
```{r, eval=TRUE}
my_df[my_df$col1== 2,  "col2"]
```
:::

## Indexing

There are also alternative, more compact ways of indexing. For example, using the **`subset()`** function:

```{r,echo=TRUE}
subset(iris, subset = Species == "setosa" & Petal.Length > 1.7)
```

<br/>

equivalent to:

```{r,echo=TRUE}

iris[iris$Species == "setosa" & iris$Petal.Length > 1.7,]

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can also select columns rather than rows with the ***`select`*** argument:

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
subset(iris, select = c(Sepal.Length, Species))
```


------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can also combine the two:

```{r,echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
#| attr-output: 'style="max-height: 250px; max-width: 80%; overflow: auto;"'
subset(iris, subset = Species == "setosa" & Sepal.Length > 4, 
       select = c(Sepal.Length, Species))
```


... equivalent to:

```{r,echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
iris[iris$Species == "setosa" & iris$Sepal.Length > 4,
     c("Sepal.Length","Species")]
```

## Indexing

Most of the time you will access variables with the **`$`** operator. This command can also be used to create a new variable...

```{r,echo=TRUE}
#| attr-output: 'style="max-height: 280px; max-width: 90%; overflow: auto;"'
# create a variable that is the sum of Length and Width
iris$sum <- iris$Sepal.Length + iris$Sepal.Width
iris[, c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width", "sum")]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The same concepts we have seen for vectors apply, so you can both create and modify variables...

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_df <- data.frame(num = 1:4, let = letters[1:4])

# Modify the num variable by adding 1
my_df$num <- my_df$num+1
my_df$num

# Create a third variable ?paste
my_df$both <- paste(my_df$num, my_df$let, sep = "_") 
my_df$both
```


## Combining Dataframes

Dataframes can be combined with the **`rbind()`** function:

```{r,echo=TRUE, error=TRUE}
# create a second dataframe
my_df2 <- data.frame(num = 4:7, lett = letters[1:4],
                    both = paste(4:7,letters[1:4], sep = "_"))

# join the two
my_df3 <- rbind(my_df,my_df2)
```

## Rules

-   The dataframes must have the same number of columns

-   The column names must be identical

```{r,echo=TRUE, error=TRUE}
str(my_df)
str(my_df2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Fix the names**

```{r,echo=TRUE, error=TRUE}
names(my_df2)
names(my_df)

# I want the names of my_df2 to match the names of my_df
names(my_df2) <- names(my_df)

my_df3 <- rbind(my_df,my_df2)
str(my_df3)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

You may also need to collect different types of data from the same participant, and then combine the collected information...

```{r, echo=TRUE}
df_rt <- data.frame(subj = factor(rep(c("alice","bob"), each = 60)),
                   cond = factor(rep(c("easy","hard"),
                                     each = 30, times = 2)),
                      rt = c(rlnorm(n = 30, meanlog = -1, sdlog = .25),
                             rlnorm(n = 30, meanlog = -.7, sdlog =.3),
                             rlnorm(n = 30, meanlog = -1, sdlog = .25),
                             rlnorm(n = 30, meanlog = -.7, sdlog =.3)))
df_rt
```

----

Dataframe containing the age:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
df_age <- data.frame(subj = factor(c("alice","bob")), age = c(20,18))
df_age
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r,echo=TRUE}
# structure of the reaction times dataframe
str(df_rt)


# structure of the age dataframe
str(df_age) 
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this case, we can use the **`merge()`** function ...

```{r, echo=TRUE}
df_all_1 <- merge(x = df_rt, y = df_age, by="subj")
df_all_1
```

----

... or the **`_join()`** function..

```{r, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr) # load the dplyr package

df_all_2 <- left_join(x = df_rt, y = df_age, by = c("subj")) 
df_all_2
```


---

```{r, echo=TRUE}
df_rt$gender <- rep(c("F","M"), each = 60)
df_age$gender <- c("F","M")

df_all_g <- merge(x = df_rt, y = df_age, by=c("subj","gender"))
df_all_g
```



## Contingency tables

We can use the **`table()`** function both to compute frequencies...

```{r, echo=TRUE}

# keep only rts between .250 and 1.5 seconds
# i.e. the rows that meet this condition
df_rt_clean <- df_rt[df_rt$rt > .25 & df_rt$rt < 1.5, ]
table(df_rt_clean$subj) # trials for each subject
table(df_rt_clean$subj, df_rt_clean$cond) # subject x condition
```

## Exporting and importing data

In R we can import data in many different formats; most commonly you will import ***.csv*** or ***.xlsx*** data.

Here, for example, I export the dataframes in two different formats...

```{r, echo=TRUE}
library(readr) # load the readr package
library(writexl) # load the writexl package

write.csv(df_rt, file = "DATA/df_rt.csv",row.names = FALSE)
write_xlsx(df_age, path = "DATA/df_age.xlsx")
```

## Importing

```{r, echo=TRUE}
library(readxl) # load the readxl package

df_rt_impo <- read_csv("DATA/df_rt.csv") # uses the readr package

df_age_impo <- read_xlsx("DATA/df_age.xlsx")
```

## Checking the structure


```{r, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE}
#| attr-output: 'style="max-height: 200px; max-width: 90%; overflow: auto;"'
str(df_rt) # Data frame we created
str(df_rt_impo) # Data frame we loaded
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The dataframe is imported as a tibble, and in this case the ***`factor`*** variables have been imported as ***`character`***. This can be changed either when importing ( **`?read_csv`** ):

```{r,echo=TRUE,message=FALSE}
df_rt_impo1 <- read_csv("DATA/df_rt.csv",
                       col_types =
                         list(col_factor(),col_factor(),
                              col_double()))
str(df_rt_impo1)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

or afterwards with the **`as.factor()`** command:

```{r,echo=TRUE,message=FALSE}
df_rt_impo$subj <- as.factor(df_rt_impo$subj)
df_rt_impo$cond <- as.factor(df_rt_impo$cond)
str(df_rt_impo)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

equivalent to:

```{r,echo=TRUE,message=FALSE}
df_rt_impo2 <- read_csv("DATA/df_rt.csv") %>% #library(tidyverse)
  mutate(subj = factor(subj),
         cond = factor(cond))
str(df_rt_impo2)
```

(just to show you that in ***R*** a problem can be solved in different ways)

------------------------------------------------------------------------


The examples I have shown concern data in formats **external** to R, but we can also save and import data in **`R`** formats.

Their main drawback is that they can be read (mainly) only within the R environment.

If we need to work with different software or languages, it is probably better to use a more generic format (e.g, .csv or .txt).
